analysis.one_liner: Requires rent-to-own stores to tell customers the total cost of owning an item and to end abusive collection practices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced in March 1994 and died there, never receiving a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let customers take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with weekly or monthly payments, and customers only own the item after paying for months or years. This bill would have amended the Consumer Credit Protection Act to force those merchants to disclose the full number and dollar amount of payments needed to own the item, the cash price, and whether the item is used or new, and to put that information on a tag attached to the product. It would also have barred contract terms like confessions of judgment and wage assignments, required stores to let customers behind on payments reinstate the agreement, set rules against harassing collection tactics, and let consumers sue merchants who violated these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of rent-to-own stores, who are disproportionately low-income households that cannot qualify for traditional credit. They would learn up front that the total of their rental payments often greatly exceeds the cash price of the item, would gain the right to reinstate a lapsed agreement instead of losing everything they paid, and could sue in federal court for violations.

how_it_helps.text: Merchants must disclose the total number and dollar amount of payments needed to acquire ownership, and must state the cash price of the item, so customers can see the true cost of the deal before signing.
Every item offered under a rent-to-own agreement must carry a point-of-sale tag showing whether it is new or used, the cash price, the payment amount, and the total payments to own it.
Contracts cannot include confessions of judgment, negotiable instruments, wage assignments, or waivers of the consumer's claims or defenses.

Customers who fall behind can reinstate the agreement by paying past-due charges within set windows — at least 90 days if they have paid 60% or more of the total — without losing the progress they made toward ownership.

Collection practices are restricted: no harassment, no obscene or abusive language, no unannounced visits at work or at inconvenient times, and merchants must stop contacting a customer who asks in writing.

Consumers can sue in any U.S. district court for willful violations, recovering actual damages plus at least $100, and advertising that mentions payments must state the total payments needed to own the item.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own merchants, who would bear the cost of new disclosures, tags, receipts, reinstatement rights, and litigation exposure. Because their business model relies on customers paying far more over time than the item's cash price, the disclosures themselves are the biggest threat to that revenue, and some compliance cost could be passed to customers.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for disclosure forms, product tags, and receipts fall on merchants and could be passed on to customers through higher payments; the bill also gives the Federal Reserve Board power to adjust or except classes of transactions.

The bill would not cap how much rent-to-own stores can charge; a fully informed customer would still typically pay far more than the cash price over the life of the agreement, only seeing the comparison in writing.

Civil liability has a one-year deadline for individual actions, and merchants are shielded if they follow Federal Reserve model forms, implement reasonable compliance procedures, or correct a disclosure violation within 15 days.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the low-income customers who use rent-to-own, the benefit is real: knowing the true total cost before signing, keeping the equity they built if a payment is missed, and protection from harassment are all things the market had not provided on its own. The honest limits are that the bill regulated the paperwork rather than the price, so customers would still pay a large premium for renting-to-own, and compliance costs could nudge prices up. On balance it was a modest, targeted consumer protection, not a restructuring of the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee on the same day, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Shelby of Alabama, joined by five other senators, introduced the bill on March 22, 1994.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction.
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed; the complete action history ends with the referral, and the 103rd Congress expired on January 3, 1995.
The bill's six sponsors split four Democrats and one Republican alongside the Democratic sponsor, but no action ever reached the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own merchants came out ahead: without federal disclosure or reinstatement requirements, they could continue selling contracts whose total cost customers learn only over time. Low-income customers continued bearing those costs.

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Conrad, Johnston, Breaux, and Faircloth
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — four Democrats and one Republican — at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 22, 1994 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rent-to-own industry
against.what_they_did: The rental-purchase industry actively fought state and federal regulation of its contracts during this era, favoring self-regulation instead.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan but small: six senators, four Democrats and two including one Republican, and no opposing votes were ever recorded because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: These stores profit from contracts where a customer pays weekly for months or years to own furniture or appliances; the bill's core requirements — a tag showing total payments to own versus the cash price, and the right to reinstate after a missed payment — strike directly at the practices that generate that premium [S3]. The industry's interest in keeping total costs undisclosed runs against the interests of its own low-income customers.

The bill amends the Consumer Credit Protection Act but applies only to rental-purchase agreements, so traditional lenders are untouched; the Federal Reserve Board gains rulemaking and enforcement duties, and assignees of rental-purchase contracts face liability only for violations apparent on the agreement's face.
